title: Namespaces and organising code
learningGoals: know how headers and source files work together

youtube.title: C++ Namespaces and Header Files Explained | C++ Programming EP 84
youtube.description: In this episode you will write a namespace, avoid name clashes and know how headers and source files work together, with Xecxec the crab. 0:00 Intro · 0:15 Namespaces and organising code · 0:45 Two namespaces · 1:25 Two drawers · 1:55 Second program · 2:57 Recap · 3:27 Bug of the Day · 4:15 Challenge · 4:35 Next episode

thumbnail.pose: Xecxec next to two labelled drawers that hold tools with the same name

scenes.animation: Tomato title card: EP sticker thuds in, title stamps with a whoosh, Xecxec scuttles in and waves; thud, whoosh, claw-click, sting
scenes.narration: Today we organise bigger programs. Namespaces stop name clashes, and header files split code across many files.

scenes.onScreen: "Namespaces and organising code": numbered lines (1. A namespace is a labelled drawer; 2. Use the double colon to open it; 3. A header holds declarations) and an analogy card: labelled drawers: two tools with one name, in two drawers
scenes.animation: Lines spring in one by one with a pop; the analogy card slides in from the right
scenes.narration: A namespace is a labelled drawer for names. Two drawers can each hold a function called area. You open a drawer with the double colon. In a bigger program, a header file holds declarations, and a source file holds the code. You compile the source files together.
points: A namespace is a labelled drawer
Use the double colon to open it

analogy.title: Namespaces and organising code
analogy.body: Labelled drawers: two tools with one name, in two drawers

scenes.onScreen: space.cpp: two area functions live in two namespaces
scenes.animation: Code types in with key-tick; butter [HL n] highlight sweeps line by line with marker-swipe; explanation card on the right
scenes.narration: [HL 4] This namespace is the circle drawer. [HL 6] It holds an area function for a radius. [HL 11] This is the square drawer. It also holds a function named area. There is no clash, because the drawers are different. [HL 18] The double colon opens the circle drawer. The area is twelve point five six six four. [HL 19] This call opens the square drawer. The area is nine.

scenes.onScreen: a table of the two namespaces and their members
scenes.animation: Table rows slide in one by one; the row the narrator mentions glows butter
scenes.narration: The circle namespace holds pi and area. The square namespace holds its own area. The double colon tells the compiler which drawer to open.

diagram.caption: a table of the two namespaces and their members

scenes.onScreen: alias.cpp: a nested namespace gets a short alias
scenes.animation: Second program or a twist on the first; [HL n] and [TRACK name=value] cues drive the variable tracker; output panel fills line by line with a ding per line
scenes.narration: [HL 4] Since C plus plus seventeen, you can write a nested namespace on one line. [HL 10] An alias gives a long name a short one. [HL 13] We call the function through the alias. The result is six point two eight three one eight.

scenes.animation: Dark-blue terminal: the compile command types with key-tick, the run command types, output prints in mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Save the file as alias dot cpp. Compile it with g plus plus. Then run the program. The program prints twelve point five six six four, nine, and then six point two eight three one eight.

scenes.animation: Recap lines tick in one by one with a pop; Xecxec nods after each tick
scenes.narration: Let us recap. One. A namespace is a labelled drawer for names. Two. Use the double colon to open a drawer. Three. A header holds declarations, and a source file holds the code. Four. Compile all source files together. Pause the video. Say these ideas out loud, one time, slowly.
points: A namespace is a labelled drawer for names.
Use the double colon to open a drawer.
A header holds declarations, and a source file holds the code.

scenes.onScreen: BUG OF THE DAY: An ambiguous call
scenes.animation: Butter banner drops in with a buzzer; wrong code shakes; the g++ error lines appear in tomato; the fix slides in and the terminal turns mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Bug of the Day. We open both namespaces, and then call area. The compiler says the call is ambiguous. Write the namespace name in front of the call.

scenes.onScreen: Why do namespaces never fight? Everyone stays in their own drawer.
scenes.animation: Full tomato screen, card flips in with a rimshot, Xecxec snaps his claw
scenes.narration: Why do namespaces never fight? Everyone stays in their own drawer.

scenes.onScreen: Task card: make a math namespace
scenes.animation: Task card pops in; checklist ticks with a pop; Xecxec holds a tiny pen
scenes.narration: Your challenge: Write a namespace called mymath with a function square. Call it from main with the double colon. Write your answer in the comments.

scenes.animation: Next-episode card slides up with a whoosh; right side stays empty for end-screen elements; sign-off text types in
scenes.narration: We end module nine here. Next time: data structures, starting with the linked list. Keep coding, says Xecxec!

bug.error:
Compiler output (exactly as g++ prints it):

ambiguous.cpp: In function 'int main()':
ambiguous.cpp:16:17: error: call of overloaded 'area(int)' is ambiguous
   16 |     cout << area(2) << endl;
      |             ~~~~^~~
ambiguous.cpp:5:8: note: candidate: 'double circle::area(double)'
    5 | double area(double r) { return 3.14159 * r * r; }
bug.why: Using namespace opens the drawers, and the names clash again. Write the namespace name in front of the call, and avoid using namespace in big programs.

pun: "Why do namespaces never fight? Everyone stays in their own drawer."
challenge: Write a namespace called mymath with a function square. Call it from main with the double colon.
challengeAnswer: Write namespace mymath, and put the function inside the braces. In main, call mymath double colon square.
